etymology: Hebrew Tser, perhaps “flint” or “rock”; one of the fenced cities of Naphtali, named once.
biblical_def: Zer was one of the fenced (fortified) cities of Naphtali, listed among the strongholds of that tribe: “And the fenced cities are Ziddim, Zer, and Hammath, Rakkath, and Chinnereth” (Josh 19:35). These fenced cities stood along the fair shore of the sea of Chinnereth (Galilee), walled against the enemy. If the name means “flint” or “rock,” it suits a fortress, hard and defensible. The fenced cities of Israel preach both a comfort and a caution. God gave His people walled towns for their safety, that they might dwell secure; the name of the LORD is a strong tower, and the righteous runneth into it and is safe. Yet Israel was warned not to trust in her fenced cities and high walls in the place of the LORD, for the strongest wall is no defence when God withdraws His protection, and the mightiest fortress falls at His word. Zer, a fenced city of Naphtali, reminds the believer that true security is not in the works of men’s hands but in the living God, who is Himself the rock and refuge of His people. Better is trust in the LORD than confidence in walls; the name of the LORD is the only tower that cannot be thrown down.

etymology: Hebrew Chali, “ornament” or “jewel”; a town on the border of Asher, named once.
biblical_def: Hali was a town on the border of Asher, listed with Helkath, Beten, and Achshaph: “And their border was Helkath, and Hali, and Beten, and Achshaph” (Josh 19:25). Its name means “ornament” or “jewel,” a fitting word for a town of Asher, the tribe of fatness and royal dainties, of whom Jacob said, “Out of Asher his bread shall be fat, and he shall yield royal dainties” (Gen 49:20), and Moses, “Let Asher be blessed with children; let him be acceptable to his brethren, and let him dip his foot in oil” (Deu 33:24). Asher was the tribe of oil and plenty and pleasant things. Hali, a “jewel” among its towns, preaches the truth that the people of God are His ornament and treasure. The LORD calls His redeemed His jewels, His peculiar treasure above all people, and in the day when He makes up His jewels He will spare them as a man spareth his own son that serveth him. The saints are the ornament of grace, decked not with gold and pearls but with the hidden man of the heart, the meek and quiet spirit which is in the sight of God of great price. Hali, a jewel-town of blessed Asher, is a token that God accounts His people precious, His special treasure and His crown of glory.

etymology: Hebrew Amad, perhaps “station” or “standing-place” (from the root “to stand”); a town of Asher, named once.
biblical_def: Amad was a town of Asher, named once with Alammelech and Misheal: “And Alammelech, and Amad, and Misheal; and reacheth to Carmel westward” (Josh 19:26). If its name comes from the Hebrew root meaning “to stand,” it is a “standing-place” or station, a settled and enduring place. It belonged to Asher, the tribe blessed with strength for its days: “Thy shoes shall be iron and brass; and as thy days, so shall thy strength be” (Deu 33:25). Amad, a “standing-place” of that tribe, preaches the grace of standing fast. The people of God are called to stand: to stand fast in the faith, to stand in the evil day having done all, to stand fast in the liberty wherewith Christ has made them free. It is God who makes them stand, for who art thou that judgest another’s servant? to his own master he standeth or falleth; yea, he shall be holden up, for God is able to make him stand. As Asher’s strength was promised equal to his days, so the standing of the saints is not in their own firmness but in the upholding hand of God, whose strength is made perfect in weakness. Amad bids the believer, having done all, to stand, in the strength that God supplies for every day.

etymology: Hebrew Chosah, “refuge” or “place of hope”; a town on the coast of Asher near Tyre; distinct from Hosah the Levite doorkeeper.
biblical_def: Hosah was a town on the sea-coast of Asher, near the great city of Tyre: “And then the coast turneth to Ramah, and to the strong city Tyre; and the coast turneth to Hosah; and the outgoings thereof are at the sea from the coast to Achzib” (Josh 19:29). This is a place, distinct from Hosah the Levite who was a doorkeeper for the ark in David’s day. The name means “refuge” or “place of hope,” from the root that gives the word so often on the psalmist’s lips: to trust, to take refuge, to hope in the LORD. A coastal town called “refuge,” set near the proud stronghold of Tyre, quietly preaches where true refuge is found. Tyre trusted in her riches and her ships and her fenced walls, and was cast down; but they that put their trust in the LORD shall never be confounded. The name of Hosah is the confession of every believing heart: in the LORD do I put my trust. He is a refuge in the day of trouble, and He knoweth them that trust in Him. As the towns of Asher looked out upon the sea, so the soul that hopes in God looks beyond the changing tide of this world to the unfailing refuge, and finds that they which take refuge in Him are like mount Zion, which cannot be removed but abideth for ever.

etymology: Hebrew Yiron, perhaps “place of fear” or “fearfulness”; a fortified town of Naphtali, named once; distinct from iron the metal.
biblical_def: Iron was a town of Naphtali, listed among its cities: “And Iron, and Migdalel, Horem, and Bethanath, and Bethshemesh; nineteen cities with their villages” (Josh 19:38). This is a place, quite distinct from iron the metal; the Hebrew name may mean “place of fear” or “fearfulness.” It stood among the cities of Naphtali in the north, the tribe blessed as “satisfied with favour, and full with the blessing of the LORD” (Deu 33:23). A town named “fear” among a people so richly blessed turns the mind to the right and holy fear of God, which is the beginning of wisdom and the companion of His favour. There is a fear that hath torment, the dread of the guilty and the terror of the wicked; and there is a fear that is clean, enduring for ever, the reverent awe of the child toward the Father, which drives out the other fear. The fear of the LORD is a fountain of life; in it is strong confidence, and His children have a place of refuge. Iron, a town of “fear” in blessed Naphtali, preaches that the fear of God and the favour of God dwell together: to fear Him is to be safe, satisfied with favour and full of His blessing, and to be delivered from every lesser and tormenting fear.

etymology: Hebrew Elon, “oak” or “terebinth”; a town in the tribe of Dan, named once; distinct from Elon the judge and Elon the Hittite.
biblical_def: Elon was a town in the lot of Dan, named once with Shaalabbin and Ajalon: “And Shaalabbin, and Ajalon, and Jethlah” — and, in the fuller list, “And Elon, and Thimnathah, and Ekron” (Josh 19:43). This is a place, distinct from Elon the judge of Israel and from Elon the Hittite, Esau’s father-in-law. The name means “oak” or “terebinth,” the great strong trees under whose shade the men of old built altars, buried their dead, and met with God. Dan was a tribe of narrow borders and restless strength, of whom Jacob said, “Dan shall judge his people, as one of the tribes of Israel” (Gen 49:16). Elon, an oak-town of Dan, preaches the strength and shelter that God gives, and the danger of the strong tree that stands alone. The oak is an emblem of the righteous, who shall be called trees of righteousness, the planting of the LORD, that He might be glorified; they flourish and spread and give shade to others. Yet Israel also sinned under the oaks, making them shrines of idolatry. The oak-town warns that strength and stature must be consecrated to God, lest they become a place of false worship; the tree that flourishes must be the LORD’s planting, or it flourishes to its own ruin.

etymology: Hebrew Yithlah, perhaps “a hanging” or “lofty place”; a town in the tribe of Dan, named once.
biblical_def: Jethlah was a town in the lot of Dan, named once with Shaalabbin and Ajalon: “And Shaalabbin, and Ajalon, and Jethlah” (Josh 19:42). Dan’s portion lay in the low country and the hills toward the Philistine plain, a narrow and hard-pressed inheritance; indeed the coast of Dan “went out too little for them,” so that part of the tribe went north and took Leshem (Josh 19:47). Jethlah, an obscure town of that cramped and restless tribe, shares in Dan’s story of a portion that seemed too small. It preaches a lesson in contentment and in the danger of grasping. Dan, dissatisfied with its lot, went far north to seize a quiet people and set up there the graven image that became a snare to Israel for generations. Discontent with God’s allotment bred idolatry and ruin. The believer is warned to be content with such things as he has, for godliness with contentment is great gain; the man who murmurs at his portion and reaches beyond the bound God has set opens the door to sin. Jethlah, a little town of hemmed-in Dan, bids the soul rest content in the place and portion the LORD has appointed, and seek its increase not by grasping but by trusting the God who gives what is good.

etymology: Hebrew Bene Beraq, “sons of lightning”; a town in the tribe of Dan, named once.
biblical_def: Bene-berak, “sons of lightning,” was a town in the lot of Dan, near the coast toward Joppa: “And Jehud, and Beneberak, and Gathrimmon” (Josh 19:45). Its striking name binds together the sons of men and the lightning of heaven. Lightning in Scripture is the token of God’s swift and dazzling power: His judgments go forth as lightning, the LORD thundereth and sendeth out His arrows, and at the last the coming of the Son of man shall be as the lightning that shineth from the east even unto the west. A town called “sons of lightning” in restless Dan preaches the suddenness and glory of the works of God. He can send help as swiftly as the lightning flash, and His judgment falls as suddenly upon the secure. The believer is bidden to watch, for the day of the Lord cometh as a thief in the night, and His appearing shall be sudden and glorious. Bene-berak, the town of the lightning-sons, is a summons to be ready, since the God who lightens the world from end to end will come in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, and the dead shall be raised and the living changed at the last trump. Blessed is that servant whom his Lord, coming as the lightning, shall find watching.

etymology: Hebrew Raqqon, perhaps “thinness” or “the temple (of the head)”; a town in the tribe of Dan, near Joppa, named once.
biblical_def: Rakkon was a town in the lot of Dan, near the sea and the border before Japho (Joppa): “And Mejarkon, and Rakkon, with the border before Japho” (Josh 19:46). It stood at the western edge of Dan’s little inheritance, where the tribe’s land ran out to the sea over against the port of Joppa. Joppa would become the harbour from which Jonah fled toward Tarshish rather than obey the LORD, and the town where Peter lodged with Simon the tanner and saw the vision that opened the door of the gospel to the Gentiles. Rakkon, a border-town looking out toward that seaward gate, quietly stands near the edge where Israel touched the wider world of the nations. It preaches that the bounds of God’s people were never meant to shut out the world for ever, but that from the seacoast of the promise the light would one day go forth to the isles and the far countries. The God who set Dan by the sea had purposed that His salvation should reach to the ends of the earth; and from Joppa, near this obscure town, the gospel first turned to the Gentiles. Rakkon on the shore is a small token of the missionary heart of God, whose word runs to the uttermost isles.

etymology: Hebrew Golan, perhaps “their captivity” or “circuit”; a city of refuge in Bashan, given to the Gershonite Levites out of the half-tribe of Manasseh.
biblical_def: Golan was a city of refuge in Bashan, one of the three set apart east of Jordan for the manslayer to flee to: “And on the other side Jordan by Jericho eastward, they assigned Bezer in the wilderness upon the plain out of the tribe of Reuben, and Ramoth in Gilead out of the tribe of Gad, and Golan in Bashan out of the tribe of Manasseh” (Josh 20:8; also Deu 4:43). It was given to the Gershonite Levites “to be a city of refuge for the slayer” (Josh 21:27). To Golan a man who had killed his neighbour unawares, without hatred, might flee and be safe from the avenger of blood until he stood before the congregation for judgment; and if found guiltless of murder, he dwelt there in safety until the death of the high priest. The cities of refuge are among the clearest gospel types in the law. They preach a sure and appointed refuge for the guilty who flee to it, safety within its bounds, and liberty at the death of the high priest — for the death of our great High Priest sets His people free for ever. Christ is the true city of refuge, to whom the soul pursued by the law and by justice may flee and find shelter; they who have fled for refuge to lay hold on the hope set before them have a strong consolation, and are safe for ever in Him.
